claims.text: The baseline material is a carbon-doped high-entropy-alloy film without deliberately engineered graphene interfaces.
Nanolayered graphene interfaces can be integrated into an HEA multilayer coating structure.
Introducing nanolayered graphene interfaces creates interfacial barriers in carbon-doped HEA films.
Graphene interfaces block dislocation motion in carbon-doped HEA films.
Blocking dislocation motion with graphene interfaces significantly delays time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained load.
The relevant comparison should be performed under sustained loading in a regime where dislocation motion governs plastic deformation.
Nanolayered graphene interfaces refine the grain structure of the HEA coating.
Graphene interfaces create structural discontinuities that obstruct dislocation motion.
A sufficiently strong barrier can make subsequent dislocation motion more difficult and require additional force for the dislocation to overcome it.
Graphene layers pin dislocations in carbon-doped HEA coatings.
Graphene interfaces force dislocations to bypass or overcome the interfaces.
Coatings containing graphene interfaces will have a lower creep rate than otherwise comparable coatings without graphene.
Post-deformation microscopy will show more evidence of pinned or blocked dislocations in graphene-containing coatings than in the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies when dislocation motion is the dominant deformation mode.
The proposed mechanism may become ineffective at extreme temperatures or stresses where alternative deformation mechanisms prevail.
The optimal graphene-layer thickness, graphene-layer distribution, and carbon concentration are not yet precisely determined.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing graphene-containing and graphene-free carbon-doped HEA coatings under otherwise identical creep conditions and examining their dislocation structures by TEM.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction or dislocation blockage in the graphene-containing coating would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The design lists deformation rate as a controlled condition, while the predicted outcome and measurements require creep strain rate to be a response variable that can differ between groups. A constant-load creep test should control load and temperature while measuring deformation rate, rather than fixing both load and deformation rate.
